# What has been read

Source PDFs are in `readings/`, which is not committed. The bibliography carries
the DOIs.

| Source | Status |
|--------|--------|
| @westphal2024eh | Read in full, 22 pp. |
| @murphy2025please | Read in full, 24 pp. |
| @liang2023gpt | Read in full, 6 pp. |
| @davies2020tour | Read in part: the corpus table and the sections on dialectal variation and virtual corpora. |
| @biber2015exploring | Not read, and will not be. Abstract only; closed access with no reachable copy. |
| @davies2015expanding | Not read. Known only through the two papers that cite it. |

Every claim below about @biber2015exploring and @davies2015expanding is a
second-hand report taken from @murphy2025please or @westphal2024eh. The final
section says what follows from not having them.

@westphal2024eh appeared online in November 2023 under a 2023 copyright line.
The version of record sits in volume 8, dated 2024, which is the year used here
and in the bibliography.

# Prior art: the operationalisation is not already done

Both GloWbE papers count a fixed lexical item across national components, which
is the shape of Study 1. Neither does what Study 1 does.

@murphy2025please covers GB and US only. She draws 1,000 random concordance
contexts per variety, codes 800 of them into twelve act-types, and tests the
resulting proportions with Pearson chi-square. Her corpus-wide frequencies are
93,356 instances of *please* in GB against 91,948 in US, or 240.85 against
237.71 per million words, a difference she treats as immaterial.

@westphal2024eh covers GB, US, CA, NZ, IN, PH, SG, NG and JM. He reports
normalised rates per million words for sentence-final *eh*, splits them by
punctuation and by text type, and reserves regression for the coding of
pragmatic function rather than for the frequency comparison.

Three gaps follow.

Neither study includes Australia, Ireland or South Africa. Three of this study's
five varieties are untouched by both.

Neither puts an interval on a cross-variety rate comparison. @murphy2025please
tests proportions within a coded sample; @westphal2024eh reports point estimates
and describes the differences qualitatively, noting himself that variety
differences in GloWbE need to be interpreted with caution. The exact Poisson
intervals and the mixed-model composite fixed in `R/analyse.R` are
more cautious about the comparison than the practice in either paper.

Neither measures anything about generated text. The link from national register
to LLM output is unmade in this literature.

# The genre control is weaker than the design assumed

The blog/general split is real and queryable. @westphal2024eh reports
sentence-final *eh* separately for blogs and general websites in all nine of his
components, and his Table 1 gives word counts for both sections of each. Gating
item 3 is answered: the interface exposes the split per variety.

The split does not separate genres cleanly. @murphy2025please states that GloWbE
has General and Blog subcategories but that @biber2015exploring found the
categories overlap too much to be useful, and on that basis she abandoned an
initial effort to balance her sample across them. @westphal2024eh keeps the
split while citing @davies2015expanding as holding that a clear distinction
between general and blog texts is not possible.

One published user of the corpus abandoned the split; the other used it with the
corpus authors' own caveat attached.

The consequence is a wording change rather than a modelling change. The
`variety:section` term and its test stand. What the section term cannot
support is the inference that a difference between varieties is therefore not a
difference between genres. Built on overlapping categories, it reduces genre
confounding without eliminating it, and anything written from these results has
to say the weaker thing.

# Corpus composition: two different blog figures

Two quantities invite conflation here. The figure of roughly 60 per cent
informal blogs is @davies2015expanding on the provenance of the texts. The
corpus's own Blog *section* is smaller, on the word counts in @westphal2024eh:

| Component | Blog | General | Total | Blog share |
|-----------|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|-----:|
| GB | 131,671,002 | 255,672,390 | 387,343,392 | 34.0% |
| US | 133,061,093 | 253,536,242 | 386,597,335 | 34.4% |

A third of the words sit in the section labelled Blog. The gap between that and
60 per cent is the overlap problem of section 3 seen from the other side:
blog-like text is spread across both sections rather than confined to one.

These totals also disagree slightly with the interface's own figures, which
@davies2020tour gives as 387.6 million words for GB and 386.8 million for US.
The discrepancy is small but it is larger than rounding, so the offsets in the
model should use section word counts read off the interface at query time, and
those figures should be recorded with the counts rather than reconstructed
later.

# Method worth adopting

**A precision check on the loose frames.** @westphal2024eh samples thirty
concordance lines per component, codes them, and reports what survives: 96.5 per
cent of his sentence-final hits were genuine pragmatic markers rather than
onomatopoeia. `data/frames.csv` marks F10 and F13 as `partial` because they will
admit false positives. They need the same treatment, and it costs queries the
plan has not budgeted.

**An exclusion list.** @murphy2025please removes duplicates, biblical, literary
and song-lyric quotation, and writers who signal a non-target dialect through
spelling or explicit reference to another nationality. Directly reusable.

**A number for the country-assignment threat.** From a spelling test on *color*,
*tumor* and *neighbor*, @murphy2025please estimates that 10–15 per cent of
writers in the GB and US subcorpora are non-nationals. That biases toward the
null: real between-variety differences are understated rather than manufactured.

**Punctuation is a searchable token.** @westphal2024eh searched *eh* followed by
a full stop, an exclamation point or a question mark. F06 and F10 depend on
matching a comma, and this confirms the interface will do it.

**Do not add part-of-speech frames.** @murphy2025please found many verb uses of
*please* mis-tagged as adverbs and abandoned the tagging. The frozen frames are
all string and wildcard patterns, so this does not bite; it is a reason not to
relax that later.

# What the detector literature establishes, and what it does not

@liang2023gpt evaluate seven detectors on 91 TOEFL essays by non-native writers
and 88 US eighth-grade essays. The average false-positive rate on the TOEFL
essays is 62.22 per cent against near zero on the eighth-grade essays; 18 of the
91 TOEFL essays are unanimously misclassified and 89 of 91 are flagged by at
least one detector. Prompting a model to enrich the word choices drops the
average false-positive rate to 11.77 per cent, and simplifying the word choices
in the American essays raises their misclassification from 5.19 to 56.65 per
cent. Perplexity is doing the work.

Two limits, both stated by the authors: they call it a pilot with relatively
small samples, and most detectors assessed use GPT-2 as the underlying model.
Anything written from this repository should carry both.

The comparison is non-native writers against American schoolchildren, never
native standard variety against native standard variety. The gap this study
claims is real.

# The interface, and what it costs

@davies2020tour settles the query budget. A single search in GloWbE returns
frequency, section size and rate per million for all twenty countries at once,
displayed as one row each for `FREQ`, `WORDS (M)` and `PER MIL`. The grid is
therefore priced per frame rather than per frame per variety.

Component sizes for the five varieties in this study, as the interface reports
them:

| Variety | Words (M) |
|---------|----------:|
| GB | 387.6 |
| US | 386.8 |
| AU | 148.2 |
| IE | 101.0 |
| ZA | 45.4 |

South Africa is the constraint. At 45.4 million words a frame occurring at 50
per million yields on the order of two thousand hits, which is ample, but the
rarer frames in the frozen set will be thin there and the intervals will show
it. Ireland is the next smallest at roughly a quarter of the GB component.

Restriction to blog or general is applied through the `Sections` control on the
search screen rather than through a separate query language, and virtual corpora
are available if a finer restriction is ever needed.

Full-text GloWbE is sold to anyone through corpusdata.org, as 95 per cent of the
text with the remainder withheld for copyright. Working from it would lift the
lexicalisation ceiling, allow the blog and general sections to be inspected
rather than trusted, and let Study 3 apply one counting routine to both corpora.
This study forgoes all of that to stay free to run and free to replicate. The
consequence is that the frozen frame set stays lexical and the density claim
stays a proxy. Neither the exact click
path for holding a section constant across all twenty countries nor the
per-account daily query limit has been verified against a live session, and the
guided tour in @davies2020tour documents neither.

The limits page on english-corpora.org sits behind the same Cloudflare challenge
as the corpus, so the free-tier figure is unverified. The one allowance
traceable to a readable source is institutional: UW-Madison states 400 searches
per faculty member and 200 per student each day under its academic licence,
which says nothing about a free account. The grid is fifteen searches if a
section can be held constant inside the one search that returns all twenty
countries, and thirty if blog and general need separate passes, so a daily limit
would have to be very low to bind. Confirm it in a live session before the
counting starts.

# What cannot be obtained, and what stands instead

@biber2015exploring is the paper behind the overlap finding in section 3, and it
reaches this study through a single footnote in @murphy2025please. Whether the
genre control is worth reporting at all, and in what language, depends on what
it actually says: how the register categories were assigned, how far coders
agreed, and whether blog is a category that failed or one that behaved like the
rest.

The abstract settles part of that and sharpens the question. The study codes
48,571 web documents drawn by random sampling from the searchable web, with each
document rated by four ordinary web users rather than by expert coders, working
down a hierarchical decision tree to a general register category and then to a
sub-register. It reports the register composition of the web and identifies
hybrid documents that combine categories. So it is a taxonomy of web registers
at large, not an audit of GloWbE's two sections, and @murphy2025please cites it
twice: at pp. 16-17 for how GloWbE was built, and in footnote 3 for the overlap.
Whether the second citation reflects a statement about GloWbE's own Blog and
General labels or her reading of the taxonomy cannot be settled without the
paper.

The paper is closed access and this study will not get it. OpenAlex records no
open location, the Northern Arizona University repository holds a record without
a deposited file, no author copy was found, and no institutional route is
available here.

So the question stays open permanently, and the wording of the genre control is
settled by decision rather than by reading. What stands: the overlap claim is
reported as @murphy2025please's account of a paper this study has not read, the
section term is described as reducing genre confounding without eliminating it,
and @westphal2024eh's own counts — both *eh* and *huh* commoner in the blog
section than the general one — are the evidence that the split separates
something real. That wording goes into the OSF registration and does not change
afterwards.

@davies2015expanding is also out of reach: the publisher paywalls it, the
academia.edu copy refuses automated access, and the author's own publications
page needs a login. It would have supplied the provenance figure in section 4
first-hand and the corpus authors' account of the country mapping. Both remain
second-hand through @westphal2024eh.
